items.title: The Mozart effect
items.claim: The 'Mozart effect' became famous after a 1993 Nature paper. What did the original study actually report?

options.text: Listening to Mozart permanently raised children's IQ
A short, narrow improvement on a spatial reasoning task in adults, lasting about 10-15 minutes

items.reveal_title: A short-lived effect on one specific task in adults
items.reveal:
Rauscher, Shaw and Ky (1993) reported a brief improvement on the Stanford-Binet paper-folding task in adult students.

The finding became 'classical music makes babies smarter' in popular media; later meta-analyses (Pietschnig et al., 2010) found little support for that broader claim.
items.why: Translating a careful experimental finding into public policy often loses its caveats.

items.title: Equal temperament's compromise
items.claim: 12-tone equal temperament (12-TET) makes all keys playable. What does it sacrifice compared to just intonation?

options.text: All intervals except the octave are slightly out of tune relative to pure ratios
It only works for one key

items.reveal_title: Every interval except the octave is mistuned
items.reveal:
12-TET divides the octave into 12 equal semitones of 100 cents each. The perfect fifth is about 2 cents flat from the pure 3:2 ratio; the major third is around 14 cents sharp from 5:4.

Most Western fixed-pitch instruments since the 19th century use it.
items.why: A practical standard often involves giving up purity for portability across keys.

items.title: Cage's 4'33 in 1952
items.claim: John Cage's 4'33 was first performed at Woodstock, NY in 1952. What is true of the score?

options.text: It instructs the performer to make no intentional sound for three movements totalling 4 minutes 33 seconds
It is a recording of silence

items.reveal:
David Tudor premiered the piece on 29 August 1952 at the Maverick Concert Hall.

Cage said his point was that no environment is ever silent; the audience's coughs, the rustle of trees and the room itself become the work.
items.why: Defining what counts as music expands the analytical toolkit for understanding sound.
